subject: Divine prophecy to Abram regarding sojourn and affliction duration (400 years)

figures.name: Duration of sojourn/affliction (years)
figures.note: All three textual traditions unanimously attest 400 years for the predicted sojourn and affliction of Abram's descendants; this is one of the rare cases of complete numerical agreement across the three major witnesses.

figures.name: Number of generations (implied)
figures.note: Genesis 15:16 specifies 'fourth generation' in all traditions, functioning as the generational correlate to the 400-year figure in 15:13; no divergence exists in this associated figure.

systematic_analysis.pattern: Genesis 15:13 presents no numerical divergences between the MT, LXX, and SP: all three traditions uniformly attest the figure of 400 years for the duration of sojourn and affliction. This stands in marked contrast to the systematic divergences found in the patriarchal chronologies of Genesis 5 and 11, where the LXX consistently adds 100 years to first-son birth ages for most antediluvian and post-diluvian patriarchs. The absence of divergence here may reflect the passage's prophetic and juridical character — a divine covenant declaration rather than a genealogical register — which may have made scribal modification less attractive or less common across all transmission communities.
systematic_analysis.pattern_plain: All three major ancient versions of the Bible agree perfectly on the 400-year figure in Genesis 15:13. Unlike the patriarchal age numbers, this prophecy was never changed between textual traditions.

theories.name: Masoretic Text Deflation
theories.summary: The MT deflation theory, associated with scholars such as Henry Green and developed rigorously by Jeremy Sexton and others, holds that the proto-MT tradition systematically reduced first-son birth ages in Genesis 5 and 11 by 100 years to undermine alternative chronological calculations. This theory has no application to Genesis 15:13, since no deflation of any kind is evidenced: all witnesses agree. The complete uniformity here actually provides a useful control case demonstrating that not all biblical numbers were subject to the editorial interventions hypothesized for the genealogical registers.
theories.summary_plain: The theory that ancient Jewish scribes deliberately lowered patriarchal ages doesn't apply here, since all versions agree on 400 years.
supporting_evidence: The absence of divergence in Gen 15:13 is consistent with MT deflation theory being confined to genealogical registers (Gen 5, 11), not prophetic oracles.
Prophetic covenant texts carry different scribal authority than genealogical lists, making editorial modification less likely in all traditions.
The unanimity of 400 years across MT, LXX, and SP suggests the figure was stable from the earliest recoverable archetype.
weaknesses: MT deflation theory is entirely inapplicable to this verse; its score reflects relevance to this specific passage only.
No textual variant of any kind is attested in the manuscript tradition for this numeral across the three traditions.
The theory cannot account for the divergence pattern (since there is none) in this verse.

theories.name: LXX Inflation
theories.summary: Some scholars (notably Jack Finegan in 'Handbook of Biblical Chronology') and critics of the MT deflation model argue that the LXX translators or their Vorlage inflated patriarchal numbers, particularly in Genesis 5 and 11, for theological or chronological reasons. In Genesis 15:13, however, the LXX (both Codex Vaticanus and Alexandrinus) reads 400 years in exact agreement with the MT and SP. This unanimity eliminates any possibility of LXX inflation being operative in this verse, and in fact reinforces that prophetic numerical statements were treated with greater fidelity than genealogical data.
theories.summary_plain: The idea that the Greek translators inflated biblical numbers doesn't apply here; the Greek Bible matches the Hebrew exactly.
supporting_evidence: Codex Vaticanus and Alexandrinus both attest τετρακόσια ἔτη (400 years), perfectly matching the MT's אַרְבַּע מֵאֹות שָׁנָה.
The Samaritan Pentateuch also reads 400 years, confirming the figure predates any textual split between Palestinian and Alexandrian traditions.
Acts 7:6 in the New Testament also cites 400 years, providing early external attestation of this uniform figure.
weaknesses: LXX inflation theory has no explanatory power for this verse due to complete unanimity.
The stability of this figure across traditions undermines any model that posits widespread LXX numerical creativity.

theories.name: Samaritan Pentateuch Harmonization
theories.summary: The SP is well known for harmonizing divergent figures with parallel texts, as demonstrated in its treatment of the post-diluvian genealogies in Genesis 11. However, in Genesis 15:13, the SP attests the same 400 years as the MT and LXX, offering no evidence of harmonistic activity. This is consistent with the observation that SP harmonization was most active in narrative and genealogical contexts where perceived inconsistencies could be smoothed; a direct divine prophecy to the patriarch carried a different kind of textual authority that inhibited modification.
theories.summary_plain: The Samaritan version sometimes changes numbers to make them fit together better, but it didn't do so here — it matches both other versions perfectly.
supporting_evidence: The SP's 400-year reading is consistent with its general faithfulness to numerals in prophetic divine-speech contexts.
No known SP manuscript tradition attests a variant numeral for this verse.
The agreement of SP with MT and LXX here is consistent with the figure being inherited from a common archetype without modification.
weaknesses: SP harmonization theory is inapplicable to this verse due to absence of any variant.
There is no parallel text in the Pentateuch that would trigger a harmonization effort for the 400-year figure specifically.

theories.name: Independent Traditions
theories.summary: The independent traditions model holds that MT, LXX, and SP reflect genuinely divergent text-historical streams, each preserving different numerical traditions derived from different scribal communities. For Genesis 15:13, however, the complete numerical uniformity suggests that this figure was not subject to independent development — or that all three traditions converged on the same value from a single original. The unanimity of 400 years across textual traditions, corroborated by New Testament citations (Acts 7:6) and by Josephus (Antiquities 2.204), strongly suggests a stable common archetype for this prophetic figure rather than independent but coincidentally identical developments.
theories.summary_plain: Even if the three biblical traditions developed somewhat independently, they all preserved the same 400-year figure, suggesting it comes from a single original source.
supporting_evidence: Josephus in Antiquities 2.204 and the New Testament in Acts 7:6 both independently corroborate the 400-year figure, indicating broad early Jewish and Christian awareness of this number.
The figure's stability across geographically and editorially distinct traditions (Palestinian, Alexandrian, Samaritan) is consistent with a stable archetype.
Ancient Near Eastern round-number conventions (multiples of 100 or 40) may have discouraged scribal alteration of this already schematic figure.
weaknesses: The model's explanatory power is limited when there is nothing to explain — unanimity is the default expectation, not a distinctive finding.
The apparent tension between Gen 15:13 (400 years) and Exodus 12:40 (430 years) in the MT has generated separate harmonization debates not resolvable from Gen 15:13 alone.

theories.name: Scribal Error
theories.summary: Scribal error as an explanatory model for numerical divergences posits that copyist mistakes (parablepsis, haplography, dittography, graphic confusion between similarly-shaped numerals in Hebrew or Greek) generated textual variants. In Genesis 15:13, the complete absence of any numerical divergence across MT, LXX, and SP eliminates scribal error as a factor in producing divergent readings. The consistency is notable precisely because 400 is a round number that could conceivably have been corrupted in transmission, yet no such corruption is attested in any major manuscript witness.
theories.summary_plain: Copying mistakes sometimes changed numbers in ancient manuscripts, but no such mistake occurred here — all manuscripts agree.
supporting_evidence: No textual apparatus for BHS (MT), Rahlfs-Hanhart (LXX), or the published SP texts records a variant for this numeral.
Round numbers like 400 are among the most stable numerals in scribal transmission due to their memorability and schematic character.
The Dead Sea Scrolls evidence, while not attesting Genesis 15 directly in surviving fragments, does not contradict the established uniformity.
weaknesses: Scribal error theory has zero applicability to this verse due to complete textual unanimity.
The absence of variants is actually evidence against, not for, scribal involvement in this figure.

theories.name: Theological Motivation
theories.summary: Theologically motivated numerical modification, whether to align with alternative chronological schemes, to emphasize exile duration, or to coordinate with Exodus chronology, has been proposed as a factor in various biblical numerical divergences. For Genesis 15:13, however, no tradition appears to have modified the 400-year figure, despite the existence of the competing 430-year figure in Exodus 12:40 (MT) — a divergence that has generated enormous exegetical and harmonization activity. The stability of 400 years in Genesis 15:13 despite this neighboring tension suggests that either the distinction between prophecy (approximate, round) and fulfillment (precise) was recognized by scribes, or that the figure was simply too authoritative — as the direct speech of God in a covenant context — to modify.
theories.summary_plain: Sometimes scribes changed numbers for religious reasons, but no one changed the 400-year prophecy, even though a related passage says 430 years — suggesting this number was considered too sacred to alter.
supporting_evidence: The distinction between Gen 15:13 (400 years) and Exod 12:40 (430 years MT; 215 years by LXX/SP calculation) was noted by ancient interpreters including Paul (Gal 3:17) who used the 430-year figure, suggesting awareness of the tension without modifying Gen 15:13.
The covenant context of Gen 15 (the 'covenant between the pieces') may have conferred special textual inviolability on its numerical content across all three transmission communities.
Philo, the Talmud (Seder Olam), and other ancient sources interpret rather than modify the 400-year figure, suggesting it was treated as authoritative across traditions.
weaknesses: The theory of theological protection cannot be positively demonstrated from manuscript evidence; it is an argument from silence.
If theological motivation could preserve a number, it could equally have motivated modification; the theory is not falsifiable for this verse.
The actual tension with Exod 12:40 (430 years) was sufficient motivation for modification, yet none occurred, which may simply reflect a stable archetype rather than any active preservation effort.

overall_assessment: Genesis 15:13 presents the exceptional and analytically significant case of complete numerical unanimity across the MT, LXX, and SP: all three traditions attest 400 years for the predicted duration of sojourn and affliction. This unanimity stands in sharp contrast to the systematic divergences documented in Genesis 5 and 11, where theories of MT deflation or LXX inflation are substantively engaged. The most compelling explanation is that the figure derives from a single stable archetype and was protected from modification by its covenant-speech character and its status as direct divine oracle — a category of text that scribal communities across the Palestinian, Alexandrian, and Samaritan transmission streams treated with unusual fidelity. The persistence of 400 years despite the adjacent tension with the 430-year sojourn figure in Exodus 12:40 (MT) further confirms that scribes interpreted rather than emended the discrepancy, providing a valuable methodological control for understanding the limits and targets of intentional numerical modification in biblical transmission.
overall_plain: All three ancient versions of Genesis 15:13 agree perfectly on 400 years, which is unusual and significant. This suggests the number was too authoritative — as part of God's direct speech in a solemn covenant — for any scribal community to change it, unlike the patriarchal ages in other chapters which were modified differently in different traditions.

bibcrit_assessment.title: Unanimous 400 years: prophetic oracle resists all textual modification
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The complete numerical unanimity of Genesis 15:13 across MT, LXX, and SP constitutes a significant datum for understanding the sociology of scribal transmission: it demonstrates that the same communities responsible for systematic numerical divergences in genealogical registers exercised radical conservatism toward direct divine speech in covenant contexts. This implies that intentional numerical modification — whether for chronological, theological, or computational reasons — was category-sensitive, targeting genealogical and narrative registers while leaving prophetic-covenantal speech largely untouched. The methodological implication for textual criticism is that theories of systematic deflation or inflation must be precisely bounded to the specific literary genres and contexts where modification is actually attested.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The fact that no ancient community ever changed this number tells us that biblical scribes were selective about which numbers they felt free to alter — prophecies from God in covenant settings were treated as untouchable, while genealogical ages were not.

_validation.confidence_note: Core textual claim of unanimity at 400 years is correct, but several specific citations and attributions need verification.

flagged_claims.claim: Josephus in Antiquities 2.204 and the New Testament in Acts 7:6 both independently corroborate the 400-year figure
flagged_claims.reason: Josephus's chronology of the Egyptian sojourn is complex; Antiquities 2.204 is in the Moses-birth narrative context. Josephus elsewhere (Ant. 2.318) gives 400 years from Abraham's arrival, but also 215 years in Egypt. The specific reference 2.204 as corroborating 400 years should be verified.

flagged_claims.claim: associated with scholars such as Henry Green and developed rigorously by Jeremy Sexton
flagged_claims.reason: William Henry Green (not 'Henry Green') is associated with critique of strict patriarchal chronology, but he did not specifically develop an MT deflation theory. Jeremy Sexton has written on patriarchal chronology, but the specific framing of 'MT deflation' is more associated with Henry Smith Jr. than Sexton.

flagged_claims.claim: Exod 12:40 (430 years MT; 215 years by LXX/SP calculation)
flagged_claims.reason: Slight imprecision: LXX and SP of Exod 12:40 read 430 years for the sojourn 'in Egypt and Canaan' (a textual expansion), not 215 years. The 215-year figure is a derived calculation, not the textual reading itself.
Seder Olam Rabbah is not part of the Talmud; it is a separate tannaitic chronological work. This is a minor categorical error.

flagged_claims.claim: Codex Vaticanus and Alexandrinus both attest τετρακόσια ἔτη (400 years)
flagged_claims.reason: The reading is correct in substance, but the exact form/word order in each codex should be verified rather than asserted as identical phrasing.

safe_claims: MT, LXX, and SP all read 400 years at Genesis 15:13
Genesis 15:16 references the 'fourth generation' in all traditions
There is a tension between Gen 15:13 (400) and Exod 12:40 (430)
Paul in Gal 3:17 uses the 430-year figure
LXX systematically diverges from MT in Genesis 5 and 11 patriarchal ages
SP is known for harmonizing tendencies elsewhere in the Pentateuch
